title: Permits and approvals
takeaway: Reject any request that mentions Permit, approval, spender or "all", unless you started that exact action on the official site.

cards.title: The free egg
cards.body: A site offers a free dragon egg to early Keepers. You connect your mint wallet. A popup asks for a quick signature with no gas fee. It feels like nothing. Read the rows before you decide.

value.label: Permit
value.why: A Permit lets a spender move your tokens.

value.label: Unknown spender
value.why: An address you do not know would get your tokens.

value.label: Unlimited amount
value.why: No limit on what can be taken.

cards.title: Permit: a signature that spends
cards.body: A Permit is a signature that lets a spender move your tokens. It costs no gas, so it feels like a login. Permit2 does the same for many tokens at once. In ScamSniffer's 2025 report, Permit and Permit2 made up about 38% of losses in the 11 cases of $1M or more.
points: Revoking later is often too late.

cards.title: Approve all
cards.body: setApprovalForAll lets one address move every NFT you hold in that collection, until you revoke it. Marketplaces use it for real listings, so approve it only when you started a listing yourself on the official marketplace. A signed listing can also sell your NFTs for 0 ETH. In 2023 one drained over $1M of NFTs from a founder's wallet.

cards.title: Warnings can miss
cards.body: Your wallet may show a red warning on known scams. Take it seriously, and never let a site talk you past it. But do not wait for one. Wallet alerts are advisory: they can miss threats, and you can still press confirm. No warning is not a green light. You read the rows. You decide.

cards.title: Try it
cards.body: A rarity checker site asks for this to rank your dragons. Tap every red flag, then tap Done flagging.

questions.stem: A free egg site asks for a gasless signature labeled Permit. What do you do?
options: Reject it, a Permit can hand over tokens
Sign it, a gasless signature cannot move funds
Sign it, then revoke it on revoke.cash later
Sign it with your hardware wallet for protection
questions.why: A Permit grants a spender your tokens. Scammers usually use it quickly, so revoking afterwards is often too late.

questions.stem: Tap every red flag, then Done.

value.label: Permit2
value.why: Grants spending rights, possibly over many tokens.

value.label: All tokens
value.why: One signature would cover every token.

value.label: Unknown spender
value.why: An address you do not know.

questions.why: Permit2, all tokens and an unknown spender on a site you did not choose. Reject: you never started that action.

questions.stem: You start a listing on the official marketplace and it asks to approve the collection. Is that expected?
options: Yes, if you started that exact listing there
No, reject every approval, even on real sites
Yes, on any site that has a market
Yes, if the site looks like the marketplace
questions.why: Marketplaces need setApprovalForAll for real listings. It belongs only to an action you started yourself on the official site.

questions.stem: Your wallet shows no warning on a request to approve all your NFTs. What does that mean?
options: Nothing, alerts can miss threats
You can go ahead and confirm
The site has been verified
The wallet checked the operator
questions.why: Wallet alerts are advisory and do not catch every threat. Judge the request yourself: approve all on a site you did not start from is a reject.

questions.stem: You opened the official swap site yourself and started a swap. It asks for a Permit2 signature. What do you do?
options: Check token and amount match your swap, then sign
Reject it, every Permit2 request is always a scam
Sign without reading, the site came from your bookmark
Sign for an unlimited amount to save gas later
questions.why: Permit2 is normal for a swap you started on the real site. Still read the token, amount and spender, and reject anything you did not ask for.

questions.stem: Tap every red flag, then Done.

value.label: Approve all
value.why: Hands over every NFT in the collection.

value.label: Collection name
value.why: Naming your collection is normal. The function is the issue.

value.label: Unknown operator
value.why: An unknown address would control your dragons.

questions.why: A ranking site has no reason to control your NFTs. setApprovalForAll to an unknown operator lets it move every dragon. Reject.

questions.stem: A "verify your dragon" site asks you to sign a marketplace order priced at 0 ETH. What happens if you sign?
options: The scammer can buy your NFTs for nothing
Nothing, an order needs gas to go through
Your dragon gets a verified badge on the site
It only lists your dragon at floor price
questions.why: A signed order lets the buyer take your NFTs at that price. In 2023 one signed order drained over $1M of NFTs from a founder's wallet.

questions.stem: Your wallet shows a red warning, but the site says "ignore it, it is a bug". What do you do?
options: Reject and leave the site
Ignore the warning as told
Sign quickly before it changes
Turn off alerts and retry
questions.why: A site that asks you to ignore a warning is a red flag on its own. Reject and leave.

questions.stem: Tap every red flag, then Done.

value.label: Listing order
value.why: A gift claim should never be a sale order.

value.label: All your NFTs
value.why: Every NFT you hold would be listed.

value.label: Zero price
value.why: Your NFTs would sell for nothing.

questions.why: The title says gift, the rows say sale of all your NFTs for 0 ETH. Read the rows, not the title.

questions.stem: A site you never used asks you to approve all tokens through Permit2. What do you do?
options: Reject it, you did not start that action
Approve, Permit2 was built by a known team
Approve, Permit2 approvals expire on their own
Approve, then revoke it on revoke.cash tonight
questions.why: Permit2 can approve several tokens at once, and phishing sites abuse that. Who built it does not matter if the request is a trap.
